prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Now spring appears, with beauty crowned And all is light and life around, Why comes not Jane? When friendship calls, Why leaves she not Augusta’s walls? Where cooling zephyrs faintly blow, Nor spread the cheering, healthful glow That glides through each awakened vein, As skimming o’er the spacious plain, We look around with joyous eye, And view no boundaries but the sky. Already April’s reign is o’er, Her evening tints delight no more; No more the violet scents the gale, No more the mist o’erspreads the vale; The lovely queen of smiles and tears, Who gave thee birth, no more appears; But blushing May, with brow serene, And vestments of a livelier green, Commands the winged choir to sing, And with wild notes the meadows ring. O come! ere all the train is gone, No more to hail thy twenty-one; That age which higher honour shares, And well become the wreath it wears. From lassitude and cities flee, And breathe the air of heaven, with me.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Now, And, Why

outputs.L1:
Now spring appears, with beauty crowned,  
And all around is light and life;  
Why comes not Jane? When friendship calls,  
Why does she not leave Augusta’s walls?  

Where cooling zephyrs faintly blow,  
Yet spread no cheering, healthful glow  
To glide through each awakened vein,  
As, skimming o’er the spacious plain,  
We look around with joyous eye  
And view no boundary but the sky.  

Already April’s reign is o’er;  
Her evening tints delight no more.  
No more the violet scents the gale,  
No more the mist o’erspreads the vale.  
The lovely queen of smiles and tears,  
Who gave thee birth, no more appears;  
But blushing May, with brow serene  
And vestments of a livelier green,  
Commands the winged choir to sing,  
And with wild notes the meadows ring.  

O come, ere all the train is gone,  
No more to hail thy twenty-one—  
That age which higher honour shares,  
And well becomes the wreath it wears.  
From lassitude and cities flee,  
And breathe the air of heaven with me.
outputs.L2:
Spring has arrived, wearing its crown of loveliness, and everything nearby is filled with brightness and vitality—so why has Jane not come? When affection summons her, why does she remain within Augusta’s walls?

There the gentle west winds may blow softly, but they cannot bring the enlivening, wholesome warmth that courses through every newly stirred vein when, gliding across the wide open plain, we gaze about us in delight and see no limit except the sky.

April has already ended its rule; its evening colors no longer charm us. The violet no longer perfumes the breeze, and the mist no longer lies over the valley. That graceful season of smiles and tears—the one in which you were born—has now disappeared.

In its place comes rosy May, calm-faced and dressed in brighter green, calling the birds to lift their voices until the fields echo with their untamed songs.

Oh, come before the whole festive season has passed, before it can no longer celebrate your twenty-first year—that age granted a greater dignity, and well suited to the garland it receives. Leave weariness and city life behind, and come breathe the open, heavenly air with me.
outputs.L3:
Spring has arrived once more, bringing with it light, life, beauty, and a renewed energy that seems to awaken every corner of nature. The days are brighter, the air is softer, and the earth appears to rejoice in its own revival. Trees are filling with leaves, flowers are opening to the sun, and the whole countryside seems alive with freshness and movement.

And yet, amid all this brightness, the speaker wonders why Jane has not come. Friendship has called to her, and the season itself seems to invite her presence, but still she remains away. The speaker feels her absence strongly, as though the joy of spring is incomplete without her companionship.

April has now passed, with its changeable skies and early blossoms, and May has arrived in fuller beauty. The green of the fields has deepened, the birds sing more freely, and the meadows are lively with growth and color. Everything in nature seems to be calling out with gladness, offering peace and pleasure to anyone willing to receive it.

For this reason, the speaker urges Jane to leave the city behind. The noise, weariness, and confinement of urban life should no longer hold her back. She is encouraged to escape its burdens and come into the open countryside, where the air is fresh, the scenery is bright, and the spirit can feel restored.

The invitation is warm and affectionate: Jane should come while there is still time to enjoy the season’s beauty. Before the celebration of her twenty-first birthday has faded into the past, she is urged to share in the happiness of spring, breathe the country air, and take part in the simple joys that friendship and nature can offer.
outputs.L4:
The poem centers on Jane’s absence at the height of spring and turns that absence into an affectionate invitation. The speaker imagines the countryside as full of life, freshness, color, and movement, yet feels that the season is incomplete without Jane there to enjoy it. Spring is presented not merely as a pleasant background but as an active force of renewal: the air is clean, the fields are bright, the flowers are opening, and the whole rural world seems ready to welcome her. Against this lively pastoral setting, the city appears confining and undesirable, a place Jane should leave behind so that she can share in the freedom and delight of nature.

Through direct address, the speaker repeatedly urges Jane to come into the countryside. The invitation feels warm and personal rather than formal; it is shaped by affection, concern, and a desire to give Jane pleasure. The natural imagery strengthens this appeal, suggesting that the countryside offers not only beauty but also restoration. Fresh air, birdsong, blossoms, and open spaces become symbols of health, happiness, and emotional renewal. The poem implies that Jane’s presence would complete the scene, making the speaker’s enjoyment of spring fuller and more meaningful.

The occasion also gives the invitation a special urgency. Jane is turning twenty-one, an important birthday associated with maturity, independence, and the beginning of adult life. The speaker suggests that such a moment should not pass unnoticed in the dullness of the city. Instead, it deserves to be marked by celebration, joy, and connection with the living world of spring. In this way, the poem links Jane’s personal milestone with the season of growth and renewal. Her birthday and the spring landscape mirror one another: both represent freshness, possibility, and the promise of life opening into something new.

Overall, the poem is both a celebration of nature and an affectionate appeal to Jane. Its pastoral imagery creates an idealized vision of the countryside as a place of beauty, health, and happiness, while its direct invitation gives the poem emotional warmth. Jane’s absence makes the speaker’s pleasure incomplete, and her birthday makes her return feel even more important. The poem therefore presents the countryside as the proper place for her to celebrate this significant moment, surrounded by the freshness and joy of spring.
outputs.L5:
**Now, And, Why**

Now is the moment we always return to. No matter what happened yesterday or what may happen tomorrow, life is experienced in the present. It is where choices are made, words are spoken, and change begins.

And is the bridge between ideas, people, and possibilities. It reminds us that life is not only one thing or another, but often many things connected. We can be strong and kind, ambitious and patient, realistic and hopeful.

Why is the question that gives meaning to action. It pushes us to understand our purpose, our decisions, and our direction. When we ask why, we look deeper than the surface and search for truth.

Together, **Now, And, Why** form a simple guide: live in the present, stay open to connection, and never stop seeking meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Jane Austen’s youthful verse inviting a friend named Jane to leave Augusta and come to the countryside in spring, mentioning April, May, and her twenty-first birthday.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Jane, quit Augusta’s proud bustle and glare,  
Its assemblies, its ribbons, its dust-laden air;  
Come haste to the fields, where the hedgerows are green,  
And Spring, in her best cap and apron, is seen.

In April the primroses peep from the ground,  
And lambkins with excellent manners abound;  
In May every orchard grows saucy with bloom,  
And lilacs make bold to perfume every room.

Let others admire the parade of the town,  
The nod, and the curtsey, the feather, the gown;  
We’ll laugh at such grandeur, and walk at our ease,  
With a book, and a bonnet, and two gossiping trees.

Your twenty-first birthday shall find you, I pray,  
Not sighing in Augusta, but merry in May;  
We’ll crown you with blossoms, pour tea with delight,  
And dance till propriety bids us good-night.

Then come, my dear Jane, for the season is kind,  
Leave beaux, bells, and brickwork a little behind;  
The countryside calls you with birds in its train—  
And I, more impatient, call louder than they.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an 18th-century-style rhyming poem where the speaker asks why Jane has not visited now that spring has arrived, contrasting city lassitude with the healthful air of open plains.
counterfactuals.output:
Why comes not Jane, now Spring, with lavish hand,  
Has strewn fresh odours o’er the smiling land?  
The hawthorn whitens, and the wanton breeze  
Sighs through the meads, and wakes the drowsy trees.  

Still dost thou linger where the city’s breath  
Steals from the cheek its rose, the eye its faith?  
Where lamps at noon a sickly lustre throw,  
And languid pleasures nurse a real woe?  

Come, gentle maid; forsake the dusty street,  
Where idle beaux and painted trifles meet.  
Here health and gladness range the open plain,  
And every gale shall call thee back again.  

The lark, high-poising in the azure air,  
Repeats thy name, and chides thy long delay;  
The brook, that sparkles through the cowslip’d lea,  
Seems made to murmur only after thee.  

Then why, dear Jane, when vernal joys invite,  
Dost thou deny the fields thy welcome sight?  
Come taste the morn, untainted, fresh, and free,  
And bring back Spring, who waits to bloom with thee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a pastoral invitation poem with heroic couplets, addressed to Jane, referencing Augusta’s walls, zephyrs, violets, April’s end, blushing May, and turning twenty-one.
counterfactuals.output:
Come, gentle Jane, where Augusta’s walls arise,  
And morning zephyrs sweeten April’s skies.  

The violets breathe beneath the budding spray,  
While April’s end gives place to blushing May.  

Now fields invite, and shepherds tune the plain,  
To hail thy twenty-one with cheerful strain.  

Then leave the town, and with the springtime run;  
Come crown the flowers, and be their fairest one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create a Regency-era birthday poem urging a young woman named Jane to escape the city and enjoy the spring countryside before the season passes?
counterfactuals.output:
**To Miss Jane, Upon Her Birthday**

Dear Jane, while chiming clocks proclaim  
The honours of thy natal name,  
Let not the town, with smoky air,  
Detain thee from the season fair.  

The park may boast its measured green,  
Its gravel walks and polished scene;  
Yet sweeter far the lanes that wind  
Where hawthorn scents the vagrant wind.  

Come, quit the rout, the lamp, the glare,  
The murmur’d news, the crowded stair;  
For Spring, with all her tender train,  
Is calling thee to field and lane.  

The primrose lifts her modest eye,  
The lark is silver in the sky,  
And every brook, in sparkling haste,  
Cries, “Beauty fades if beauty’s waste!”  

Then fly, dear Jane, while blossoms stay,  
Before the lilac drops away;  
For birthdays, like the flowers of May,  
Are sweetest ere they pass from day.  

May health attend thy rural round,  
May joy in every hedge be found;  
And may this year, so fair begun,  
Bloom bright beneath the country sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical old-fashioned poem beginning with spring’s beauty and ending with an appeal to “breathe the air of heaven, with me,” addressed to an absent friend named Jane.
counterfactuals.output:
The spring hath strewn her silver dew  
On violet-bank and budding tree,  
And every lark that cleaves the blue  
Sings tidings sweet of joy to me.  

The primrose lifts her gentle face,  
The brook goes laughing through the lea,  
And all the world is touched with grace—  
But thou art far away, my Jane, from me.  

I wander where the hawthorns blow,  
Where once thy light step crossed the green;  
The same soft winds around me flow,  
Yet not the same is all the scene.  

For what are blooms, though bright they rise,  
Or birds that make the morning free,  
If I may not behold thine eyes,  
Nor hear thy voice beneath the tree?  

Come back, ere summer’s roses burn,  
Ere fades the May from field and plain;  
O let thy truant footsteps turn  
To these old paths of ours again.  

Then shall the earth more fair appear,  
The skies more deeply blue shall be;  
Come, absent friend, my Jane most dear—  
breathe the air of heaven, with me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
